name: Erica Lanka Borba
title: Erica Lanka Borba: Beyond Borders
dek: She came to Sri Lanka three years ago as a doubtful tourist, opened an account for her family in Brazil, wrote four songs and began arguing, gently, with the island's reputation.
excerpt: Erica Lanka Borba arrived in Sri Lanka as a sceptical tourist and found a country unlike the one she had been warned about. Her rule since: nobody pays for what she says about it.
seoDescription: Brazilian creator Erica Lanka Borba on Sri Lanka, her four songs, the Lotus Tower and why she will not be paid to promote the island.
content:
Erica Lanka Borba first came to Sri Lanka three years ago as a tourist, and a sceptical one. What she knew of the island had come from outside it: international reports, travel advisories, the picture of a country drawn by people who had not been there. She admits she believed some of it. Then she arrived. “I discovered a completely different Sri Lanka from the one I had imagined,” she says.

The climate was tropical and the landscapes reminded her of home, in Brazil. She felt comfortable from the first days. What kept her was the people. She has visited many holiday destinations, and she talks about their kindness long before she gets to the beaches. It comes, in her words, “from within. From the heart. From love.” Not because they expect something in return.

An account for the family

The account was not a strategy. Back home, friends and family were still doubtful about Sri Lanka, even after hearing about her trip. So she opened a social media account to show them what the country was really like. That was the whole plan. The audience that came afterwards was nobody's plan. When the media began calling her “Erica Lanka, the viral phenomenon,” she found it a little unbelievable. She still does. “Maybe the secret is that I never actually set out to reach a huge audience in the first place.”

She keeps one rule. The content she makes about Sri Lanka comes from her own passion and conviction, not from paid advertising agreements, and she means to keep it that way. Nobody paying her gets to decide what she says, what she shows or how she feels. “I'm not here to sell Sri Lanka,” she says.

A song for a tower

The music started the same way. Some feelings were too big to keep to herself, and music gave them a voice. She is firm that she is not a big music star and does not dream of becoming one. There are four songs: “Hari Hari Sri Lanka,” “Lotus Tower – Feeling the Power,” “From Rio to Colombo” and “Patricia Lanka.”

The Lotus Tower song is the one people ask about. She fell for the building the way she fell for the country, without meaning to. Many listeners abroad have never heard of it and ask her what it is. She likes that. Every question is another reason to come and see it, especially at night, when it lights up in colour.

Respect, for her, runs both ways. A media article once asked how far Erica Lanka could actually go. On a Sri Lankan beach she wears a bikini, partly to show visitors that they can; some people abroad still think they have to cover up. At a Buddhist or Hindu temple she learns the customs and dresses for them. At a gala dinner she dresses for a gala dinner. “Respecting another culture doesn't mean you have to give up your own identity.”

Quality, not numbers

She has no grand plan for the future, and says so. None of this was planned. What she wants for the island is quality tourism, thoughtful and respectful, not mass tourism. Her concern is what could happen to the warmth of its people if the numbers ever overwhelm them and that kindness gives way to commercial thinking.

Her argument is simple. “Sri Lanka doesn't need to change who it is. What needs to change is the way the outside world sees Sri Lanka!” If her music and videos bring even a few people to see it for themselves, she says, her dream has already come true.

pullQuote.text: I never want someone telling me what I should say, what I should show, or how I should feel just because they're paying me.
